newsitem.title: UK: Dollar rides higher in Europe on US treasury rally.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rides higher in Europe on US treasury rally.

text.p: The dollar continued its relentless climb higher in European trade on Tuesday, soaring past the psychological barrier of 121 yen on the back of a strong U.S. Treasury rally.

A benign fourth quarter U.S. Employment Cost Index (ECI) -- an important guage of the labour market -- dampened expectations of a February U.S. interest rate rise, sending Treasuries sharply higher, dealers said.
"The data was not dollar positive, but the Treasury rally was a relief reaction," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago in London. "And the dollar followed it higher."
"That is a bit of a contradiction, but stronger Treasuries mean greater fund flows into the U.S. and that is dollar positive."
The market had been closely watching the ECI figure for signs of increasing tightness in the U.S. labour market, which could signal an imminent rate hike, dealers said.
The ECI rose 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter versus an average forecast by economists of 0.9 percent.
The dollar received a further boost after U.S. consumer confidence jumped to a decade high 116.8 in January versus a revised 114.2 in December.
At 1620 GMT the dollar traded at 121.15 yen, off its fresh 47-month high of 121.51 but well above its 119.46 yen level in late Europe on Monday.
Lack of action from the Bank of Japan after the dollar breached 121 yen helped underpin the dollar, dealers said.
The dollar also gained on the mark, trading at a 31-month high of 1.6481 marks versus 1.6442 at the previous close.
But profit-taking and exporter sales close to the session high dragged it lower, dealers said.
This pulled mark/yen higher to a session high of 73.46 yen.
"Whilst dollar/yen has roared, dollar/mark has really been unable to rally, which is why mark/yen has gone so high today," said a dealer at a UK bank.
Knuthsen said the dollar could hit 130 yen before encountering significant resistance. "The market is still in a bullish dollar environment."
However, he said there was a risk that the Japanese could seek concerted action at the meeting of Group of Seven (G7) finance ministers in Berlin on February 8.
"I don't think Japan is concerned about the direction of the yen, but the speed at which it takes place," said Knuthsen.
A sharp slide in the yen could reverberate through the Japanese stock and bond markets.
But historically low interest rates and sluggish economies in both Japan and Germany would continue lending support to the dollar, analysts said.
"They need some sort of stimulus, but the only thing they can really do is allow their currencies to depreciate to boost exports," Knuthsen said.
Tuesday's benign wage data sent U.S. stocks and bonds broadly higher, with the Dow Jones Industrial average gaining more than 85 points and Treasuries climbing more than one point.
A flood of U.S. data later in the week will provide a good picture of the economy, analysts said, particularly fourth quarter gross domestic product (GDP) due on Friday.
This comes just before next week's meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the body of the U.S. Federal Reserve charged with setting interest rate policy.
"This week is a crucial one," said Knuthsen. "It should clearly hammer in the message that we have an economy growing above trend with wages rising."
"And that means the Fed will tighten."
